citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
Daily observation of a dairy cow to assess its health and well-being is not being done adequately. “Bessie,” a dairy cow,
was found in a thin body condition with her ribs, including the short ribs located over the abdomen, visible. The licensee
had not identified this condition and therefore, had not communicated with the veterinarian. When asked about this cow,
the licensee stated she looked fine and always looked that way. Upon interview with the attending veterinarian, he agreed
he was not aware of this cow's body condition and stated he had not seen her since June 2026. Failure to identify this
health issue delayed timely communication with the attending veterinarian and led to treatment delay, which may
negatively impact the health and well-being of this cow. The licensee must conduct thorough daily observations of all the
animals to assess their health and well-being, as well as maintain direct and frequent communication with the veterinarian
so that timely and accurate information on problems of animal health, behavior, and well-being is conveyed. The cow
identified above needs to be assessed by the veterinarian for a treatment plan.
Correct by 09/20/2026.

At the time of inspection, the acquisition and disposition records were again not current or complete. The acquisition of
animals obtained (a camel, zebus, pigs) and those disposed of (cows, goats, sheep, water buffalo) were not available and
therefore missing all of the following: dates of acquisition or disposition, names and addresses of whom the animals were
acquired from or transferred to, their USDA license number and/or Driver’s license number with state of issuance. Other
animals (goats, nilgai, and zebu) were born on property but not properly documented with full dates of birth. Without
records which fully disclose the animal’s acquisition as well as disposition information, legal and medical information
traceback is not possible. The facility shall ensure that it makes, keeps, and maintains records which fully and correctly
disclose the following information concerning all exhibition animals: the date of the acquisition or disposition, the species
and quantity of animals involved, the name, address, and USDA number, if applicable, of the person from whom the
animal was acquired from or given to, or the vehicle license number and state, as well as the driver’s license number and
state of the person, if not licensed or registered with the Animal Welfare Act. The records shall include any offspring born
of any animal while in his or her possession or under his or her control.

A safe and effective program for the control of mammalian pests is not maintained. Many of the darker colored hoofstock
(mainly the black cows) and one male nilgai in the pastures had an excessive number of flies on them. The flies were
observed swarming on and around those animals. A male nilgai appeared restless by twitching his skin where the flies
landed on his sides, flicking his ears and head back towards his body, and swishing his tail vigorously. A mostly black
dairy cow had at least 300 flies on one side of her body and was flicking her head towards the flies located at her sides.
Flies may spread disease and can be a source of irritation and cause distress to the animals. Currently, an insect growth
regulator is incorporated into the animals feed and topical treatments are given once every 2 months. The last treatment
was two months ago, per the licensee, so another treatment was due. A safe and effective program for the control of
insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
Correct by: 09/30/2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensee.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
